Letters: School district not listening to residents | The ‘People’s Mayor’ | BBQ fundraiser success | Response to ‘Anti-Jewish libel’

PUSD not listening to residents

Regarding the article on new school facilities for PUSD, I am glad to read that Superintendent Ghysels says that the way schools look can make a difference for all Pleasanton residents.

However, the school board has not listened to the residents surrounding Harvest Park Middle School who have been very patient in attending meetings and asking that no green space is lost at Northway and Valley Avenue, and that new facilities/programs do not bring in 200 more cars daily to the school.

Harvest Park is the oldest middle school with the smallest footprint, and is one of the only schools completely surrounded by residential housing. Traffic is already at very high levels and it is especially a burden to parents and neighbors during school time.

Green space is precious and is important not only to students, but to all Pleasanton residents. Other PUSD facilities have space that any additional programs can accommodate.

The walkway on Greenwood Road along the Harvest Park fence line belongs to PUSD and is cracked, uneven and hazardous. It would be great to see the district focus on improving school areas that are an eyesore and safety burden to all residents who use school sidewalks and any child walking or riding a bike to school.

– Tessie Wagner-Pease

Response to letter on ‘Anti-Jewish libel’

I would not have as much of a problem with AIPAC if they were presenting arguments in favor of certain Israeli policies, or explaining why we should be sending Israel billions of dollars in military aid. But they are not coming here to talk about that. 

They are being intentionally deceptive, using shell PACs to hide the source of their funding. They are attacking Wahab as “soft on crime”, as if locking everyone in prison would give us a better outcome. I think it only fair to call them out because they have a track record of surreptitiously interfering with elections and only later boasting of their wins when they are fundraising. 

The idea in last week’s letter that: “Those who highlight AIPAC and only AIPAC are — whether intentionally or not — using the ancient anti-Jewish libel that says Jews are some shadowy demonic force controlling the puppet strings of, well, everyone.” Applies pretty well to AIPAC. 

No one is accusing Jews, many of whom criticize the policies of Israel. People deserve to know if they are being played as pawns in some weaponized psychological war. 

I urge readers to look into the conflict in Israel, and understand that concern for the rights of Palestinians is not all that radical, unless you are AIPAC who wants nothing less than unconditional support for the state of Israel.

– John Williams

BBQ fundraiser success

The recent barbecue and auction fundraiser by the Pleasanton Community of Character Collaborative was a great success.

Scholarships were first awarded in 2012, established to honor the legacy of Juanita Haugen, longtime school board member who passed away after a battle with cancer in 2007. From then until 2023, one or two scholarships were awarded to seniors at each PUSD high school, honoring students who demonstrated exceptional character and service to their family, school and community.  

A few years ago, a small backyard barbecue was held to augment the funding of scholarships. The past three years the event has grown; this year’s event earned $24,000, with nearly 130 attendees. Due to this success, the number of scholarships has also increased to 14 this current year, awarded to PUSD seniors.

Many thanks to the board of directors, who planned, obtained auction items, cooked and served the food. Thanks to Craig and Kim Eicher for hosting in their beautiful backyard. Board members donate most of the food and other expenses for the dinner, so, nearly all of the proceeds go toward scholarships. 

Thanks to those who attended and for their generous donations, as well as community groups and companies who made donations of items and certificates for auction items. Local band Rusty Vinyl donated their time playing at the event.

Support is also provided for other community events, such as the Make a Difference Volunteer Festival, the Annual Community Thanksgiving Dinner, the Martin Luther Legacy Breakfast, Adopt a Senior at Christmas and other worthwhile events.

– Ken Mano

On ‘masked men’

As Pleasanton police Lt. Nicholas Albert was quoted in the article, there is no “expectation of privacy” that protects citizens from being photographed without consent in public places such as sidewalks, roadways, parking lots, or building entrances. 

By the same token, there is nothing prohibiting citizens from passively blocking a photographer’s view in these locations.

If “First Amendment auditors” choose to exercise their right to photograph people without consent in public settings, I would not be surprised to see groups of privacy advocates begin to organize to passively surround the “auditors”, blocking their cameras’ ability to record anything other than the advocates’ smiling faces or the backs of their heads.

Who knows? These events could evolve into joyous celebrations of the respect we all share for our revered First Amendment!

– Glenn Evans

The would-be ‘People’s Mayor’

What do you get when an elected official knows the boss is their constituents?

What do you get when an elected official always officiates based on what’s in the best interest of their constituents and enhances their quality of life?

What do you get when an elected official is not pressured or sueded by special or corporate interests?

What do you get when an elected official always listens first to constituents, answers their questions with maximum transparency before making decisions? Who always fights on behalf of their constituents despite challenging odds and at times being a minority vote?

What do you get when an elected official accepts donations from constituents and not from corporate or questionable PAC money?

What you get is a person with all the above attributes. A super smart rare breed of an elected official who is transparent and honest, works hard every day for constituents, has no hidden agendas, has a wonderful sense of humor, loves and helps their family, friends and neighbors, a limitless community advocate, and has a great smile and a warm hug at the ready. 

That’s a person people trust and is trustworthy. That person would be a People’s representative. Julie Testa is that person. 

She has been the People’s Councilmember in Pleasanton, putting people first. Her actions and voting records prove it. She is now running for Mayor of Pleasanton. She is the best choice and will absolutely be the quintessential “People’s Mayor”. Vote for Julie Testa on Nov. 3.

– Shirley Lewandowski

Project Genesis at LLNL: AI oversight gap

The Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission will use artificial intelligence to speed up scientific research and “national security” work. The White House compares its urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project: the program that created the first atomic bomb. 

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, already a central part of the U.S. nuclear weapons complex, will play a major role.

That should alarm us. LLNL-led projects will use AI in many ways. DOE talks about working faster as though faster always means better. At a nuclear weapons laboratory, it does not.

Safety depends on careful human judgment and time. AI cannot understand the actual conditions inside an aging nuclear facility. It may miss failing equipment, inadequate staffing, poor training, waste-handling problems, or other work happening nearby. 

If LLNL uses AI to rush safety reviews or experiments, workers and surrounding communities will bear the risk.

LLNL already operates behind enormous secrecy. AI could make its decisions even harder for workers, regulators, and the public to understand or challenge. It could also allow the Lab to design and modernize nuclear weapons faster while avoiding meaningful public oversight.

This is especially dangerous now that New START, the last major treaty limiting U.S. and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals, has expired. Pope Leo XIV called for a concrete and effective replacement and warned leaders to do everything possible to prevent a new arms race. Genesis must not be allowed to fuel that race.

LLNL and DOE must publicly explain how AI will be used and require independent safety reviews for every high-risk decision. Technology should be used to protect life; not to build nuclear weapons faster.

– Felicia Ziomek, Livermore

What 4% looks like from the inside

When I was 5, I asked my parents if I could put on a talent show. I had heard that children could get cancer and I couldn’t put it down.

My mom set up 30 folding chairs at my guitar school and we sold baked goods. We raised $1,980, and I thought we had probably solved it.

That was 11 years ago. I have run it every year since, including through the pandemic. I am a senior at Palo Alto High School now, and every dollar has gone to pediatric cancer research at Lucile Packard Children’s Hospital Stanford.

Somewhere in there I stopped being a kid doing a nice thing and read the research. About 4% of federal cancer research funding goes to childhood cancers. Roughly 15,000 American kids and teenagers are diagnosed every year, and cancer is still their leading cause of death by disease. 

Survival climbed from about 63% in the 1970s to 87% today, entirely because someone paid for research. The remaining 13% are the hardest cases, and they are last in line.

A talent show run by a high schooler should not be a meaningful funding source for a major hospital. That it is says something about a gap, not about me.

The 12th show is Saturday, Sept. 12, 1-3 p.m. at Valencia Park in Santana Row, San Jose. It is free, Tri-Valley families are welcome, and kids aged 5 to 18 can still sign up to perform at byebyekidscancer.org.

– Aeshaan Singhal, founder, Bye Bye Kids Cancer
